⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

Inside the cluster, OpenDefence services talk plain HTTP to each other — and every one of those calls is transparently wrapped in mutual TLS by a Linkerd service mesh whose certificates chain to the same platform CA that signs everything else. This page explains how the mesh is wired to the platform PKI, how workloads prove and pin each other's identity, and exactly which pods are (and are not) meshed.

Why a mesh

Linkerd works by injecting a linkerd-proxy sidecar into each participating pod. The application keeps speaking plain HTTP to localhost; the sidecars establish mutual TLS between themselves, verify each other's certificates against a shared trust root, and hand the peer's cryptographic identity to the receiving application. That is the entire reason it is here: none of the OpenDefence services has to implement TLS, certificate rotation, or peer verification for in-cluster traffic — the mesh applies all three uniformly, per pod, at injection time.

On this platform the mesh is not an add-on; it is load-bearing infrastructure that other components assume exists:

  • Encryption and identity for hub-and-spoke traffic. All calls between rmapi and the product integration APIs (takrmapi, mtxrmapi, matrixrmapi) are plain HTTP on URLs like http://tak-server.app-tak.svc.cluster.local:8003/, secured only by the mesh. See Integration pattern.
  • Authentication. Product APIs decide whether a caller is really rmapi by checking its Linkerd identity — the in-cluster counterpart of the callsign checks Traefik performs at the edge (Edge mTLS & callsign checks).

Because meshing happens at pod creation, ordering matters. Linkerd is installed in the infra-phase3 deploy phase (together with opendefence-pki, from k8s/main/<env>/infra-phase3/), after cert-manager (phase 1) and trust-manager (phase 2) exist to feed it certificates — and before any meshed workload. The taskfile's apply loop then blocks on the control plane being ready:

kubectl rollout status deployment linkerd-proxy-injector -n linkerd --timeout=180s
kubectl rollout status deployment linkerd-identity       -n linkerd --timeout=180s
kubectl rollout status deployment linkerd-destination    -n linkerd --timeout=180s

Only after these gates pass does the opendefence phase deploy rmapi, Keycloak and the rest — so every workload is admitted through a live proxy-injector and gets its sidecar on first creation, never as a retrofit. Injection is opt-in per Deployment — no application namespace carries a namespace-wide linkerd.io/inject annotation (the only namespace-level one is on the linkerd-viz extension's own namespace). See Deployment model for the full phase sequence.

External CA wiring

The platform pins Linkerd stable-2.14 (CLI stable-2.14.10 in mise.toml) and installs it from k8s/linkerd/base/kustomization.yaml as two inflated Helm charts: linkerd-crds 1.8.0 (with enableHttpRoutes: false, because Traefik already installs the Gateway API CRDs) and linkerd-control-plane 1.16.11. The control-plane values are where the platform diverges from a stock install:

identity:
  externalCA: true
  issuer:
    scheme: kubernetes.io/tls
disableHeartBeat: true

identity.externalCA: true means Linkerd does not generate or own its identity CA (and disableHeartBeat keeps it from phoning home — relevant for the air-gapped Zarf flavor). Instead, the identity issuer is an ordinary cert-manager Certificate named linkerd-identity-issuer (in k8s/linkerd/base/), signed by the platform's root-CA-backed ClusterIssuer ca-issuer:

spec:
  isCA: true
  commonName: identity.linkerd.cluster.local
  secretName: linkerd-identity-issuer
  duration: 48h
  renewBefore: 25h
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
  issuerRef:
    name: ca-issuer
    kind: ClusterIssuer

cert-manager keeps that issuer certificate fresh forever: each cert lives 48 hours and is re-issued when 25 hours of validity remain (roughly daily), and the linkerd-identity controller watches the kubernetes.io/tls Secret and picks up each rotation without restarts. There is no manual linkerd upgrade --identity-* ceremony and no long-lived issuer key sitting in a repo. Because ca-issuer signs with the platform root key, the mesh issuer is a direct child of the root — a sibling of the edge's intermediate-ca, not a descendant of it.

Trust anchors arrive by a parallel route: a trust-manager Bundle named linkerd-identity-trust-roots copies the root CA certificate (ca-secret's tls.crt) into a ConfigMap of the same name (key ca-bundle.crt), targeted only at the linkerd namespace via a namespace selector. Note the asymmetry with the edge: this bundle contains the root cert only, not the root+intermediate ca-bundle used everywhere else — the mesh issuer chains directly to the root, so the root alone is sufficient to validate every proxy certificate. If the platform root is ever re-keyed, both the issuer Certificate and the trust bundle regenerate from the same source; there is no separately managed mesh CA to forget.

The following diagram shows the full wiring from the platform CA through the control plane to the injected pods.

blocks.html:
Workload identity and pinning

Every proxy certificate encodes the pod's ServiceAccount as its identity, using Linkerd's CN scheme:

Most meshed Deployments run under their own ServiceAccount (rmapi, keycloak and openldap in opendefence-system; tak, mtx and matrix in their app namespaces), so identities are per-workload. One rough edge: an rmui ServiceAccount object exists, but the rmui Deployment never sets serviceAccountName, so its pods actually run — and get their mesh identity — as default.

Workload Mesh identity
rmapi rmapi.opendefence-system.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local
tak-server (via SA tak) tak.app-tak.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local
mtx-server (via SA mtx) mtx.app-mtx.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local
matrix matrix.app-matrix.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local

The platform then turns identity into authentication by pinning, and the pinning is mutual:

  • Products pin rmapi. Each product's kraftwerk-init.json (mounted at /pvarki) carries "certcn": "rmapi.opendefence-system.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local" next to rmapi's in-cluster URL, and the integration container sets MTLS_TRUST_L5D=true — telling the integration framework to accept the mesh-asserted caller identity in place of a raw client certificate, and to require that it matches the pinned CN.
  • rmapi pins the products. rmapi's own registry, the kraftwerk-rasenmaeher-init ConfigMap, stores the expected certcn (tak.app-tak.…, mtx.app-mtx.…, matrix.app-matrix.…) alongside each product URL, and rmapi's env (the rmapi-env ConfigMap) also sets MTLS_TRUST_L5D=true.

Mechanically, the receiving pod's inbound proxy terminates the mTLS connection, validates the client certificate against the root trust anchor, and forwards the request to the local app with the verified caller identity attached as the l5d-client-id header. That header is only trustworthy because it can only come from the local sidecar: at the network edge, Traefik's strip-identity-headers middleware deletes any client-supplied l5d-client-id (along with the callsign and legacy mTLS headers) before a request enters the cluster — see Ingress & network edge. There are no Linkerd Server/AuthorizationPolicy resources in the repo; authorization is enforced in application code by this CN comparison.

This sequence shows a concrete hub-to-spoke call, rmapi provisioning something on takrmapi.

The design is deliberately symmetric with the edge: outside the cluster, Traefik verifies an end-user client certificate and asserts a validated callsign; inside, the mesh verifies a workload certificate and asserts a validated ServiceAccount CN. Same CA, same pattern, two planes — see Edge mTLS & callsign checks and Integration pattern.

One PKI, two trust planes

Both planes hang off the same root created by opendefence-pki, but they branch immediately: the ~5-year intermediate-ca (and its intermediate-ca-issuer) serves the edge — host server certificates and end-user client certificates — while the 48-hour linkerd-identity-issuer serves the mesh. The two issuing CAs are siblings under the root, and their trust stores differ accordingly (edge verifiers trust the root+intermediate ca-bundle; the mesh trusts the root alone). This diagram maps the split; the full chain is covered in PKI & trust.

What is and isn't meshed

Injection is explicit and per-Deployment — pod annotations linkerd.io/inject: enabled plus config.linkerd.io/proxy-await: enabled (the app containers wait for the proxy before starting). Current coverage:

Workload Namespace Meshed Ports bypassing the proxy
rmapi, rmui opendefence-system yes none
keycloak opendefence-system yes opaque 9443 (its own TLS edge listener)
openldap opendefence-system yes opaque 1389,1636 (LDAP/LDAPS, not HTTP)
tak-server app-tak yes skip inbound 8089,8090,8091,8092,8093,8094,8443,9000,9001,9002 (TAK's own TLS client ports)
mtx-server app-mtx yes skip inbound 1936,8322,8890,9888,9889,9996,9997 (media protocols; local overlay adds debug 9998,9999)
matrix app-matrix yes skip inbound 3478,5349,7881,7882 (TURN/RTC media), skip outbound 9443
battlelog app-battlelog no not injected at all
CNPG database pods all app namespaces no operator-managed, never injected
Traefik traefik-system no edge proxy runs outside the mesh

The pattern behind the exclusions: the mesh carries the plain-HTTP API traffic (integration APIs, rmapi, Keycloak's HTTP port, the UI nginx containers), while anything that brings its own TLS or its own non-HTTP protocol bypasses the proxy. Keycloak's 9443 listener is marked config.linkerd.io/opaque-ports: "9443" — the manifest comment says it plainly: "Keycloak serves its own TLS on 9443 — keep it opaque so Linkerd passes it through as TCP" (it is the kc.<domain>:9443 edge endpoint). Correspondingly, the matrix pod skips outbound 9443 so MAS's OIDC bootstrap call to Keycloak's public listener does not go through the proxy. TAK's raw client ports are skipped with an in-repo comment reading "Only takrmapi via linkerd for the time being" — TAK clients hold their own certificates and connect over TAK's own TLS.

Honest edges to be aware of: battlelog is entirely unmeshed (its traffic arrives only via Traefik's bl.<domain> route, protected by mtls-strict at the edge, but its in-cluster hop is unencrypted plain HTTP). Database connections do not traverse the mesh either — CNPG pods are not injected, so Postgres traffic is outside Linkerd's mTLS. And because Traefik itself is unmeshed, the Traefik-to-backend hop is not Linkerd-encrypted (except where the backend speaks its own TLS, as Keycloak does); mesh mTLS covers pod-to-pod traffic between meshed workloads, which today means the hub-and-spoke API calls.

linkerd-viz

The linkerd-viz extension (Helm chart 30.12.11, namespace linkerd-viz) is deployed in the monitoring phase, not with the control plane — it is observability tooling, not infrastructure the apps depend on. It is installed with prometheus.enabled: false and prometheusUrl: http://prometheus-operated.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090, so instead of shipping its own bundled Prometheus it reuses the cluster's prometheus-operator instance. The scrape side lives in k8s/monitoring-prometheus/base/resources/linkerd-scrapeconfigs.yaml as three ScrapeConfig resources (linkerd-controller, linkerd-proxy, linkerd-service-mirror — the last a no-op on this single-cluster install, kept for parity with upstream) ported from Linkerd's external-Prometheus reference config and labeled monitoring: prometheus so the Prometheus CR selects them. Per-proxy golden metrics therefore land in the same Prometheus that Grafana and Alertmanager already use; how that pipeline fits together is covered in Observability pipeline.
